sections.h2: New Orleans is the parish, and it sits below the water
sections.html:
The city of New Orleans and Orleans Parish share the same boundaries, so one set of offices serves every address. The ground is what sets a house here apart. The city's average elevation is between 1 and 2 feet below sea level. Parts of Uptown reach about 20 feet at the base of the river levee, while the far reaches of Eastern New Orleans sit as low as 7 feet below sea level. Levees and drainage pumps hold the water back.

Hurricane Katrina in August 2005 flooded more than 80 percent of the city. Buyers and insurers remember that, so your address, lot elevation and flood history come up early in any talk about price and timing. The city's population estimate for July 1, 2025 is 362,154.

Six things tend to decide how smoothly a New Orleans sale goes: street elevation, the condition of the roof and foundation, open code cases, recorded liens, rental history and the tax bill. The paperwork side comes down to these numbers.

sections.h2: How a sale gets recorded in Orleans Parish
sections.html:
Every sale of New Orleans real estate is recorded with the Clerk of Civil District Court in its Land Records Division. State law makes that office responsible for preserving the parish property records forever and keeping them open to the public.

The old separate filing fees for mortgages, conveyances and notarial archives have been folded into a single recording fee. Checks are made payable to the Clerk of Court. In practice your notary or title company carries the signed act of sale to the clerk and pays from closing funds, but you should know where it goes and what it costs.

This is a city tax collected by the Notarial Archives on documents that transfer real estate. It applies to sales, donations, transfers, mortgages and commercial leases, and the seller is one of the parties responsible for paying it.

The tax is a flat $325 for most of these documents, due at recording. If it is not paid then, a billing form has to be filled out and the tax paid within 30 days, or interest and a $500 penalty are added. A single family residence or residential double whose document runs past 25 pages still pays $325, as long as a notarized statement confirms it is an owner-occupied single family residence or residential double.

A flat amount is easy to budget. Sellers get caught on the deadline, so settle in writing at the closing table who is paying it.

sections.h2: What happens when a house has code enforcement problems?
sections.html:
Open code cases and recorded liens follow the property, not the owner, so they have to be dealt with before or at a sale. The Department of Code Enforcement works through a set order of steps. It helps to know them if you inherited a house or lived elsewhere while it sat vacant.

  • Neighbors or inspectors report the property, and a case opens in the city's LAMA system. The target time from complaint to inspection is 30 days.
  • The Hearings Bureau researches title to find every owner and legal interest, then mails and posts a Notice of Noncompliance with a deadline to fix the violations.
  • If the violations are still open, a hearing is set 30 to 45 days after the compliance period. Owners must appear or send a representative, and hearing costs can be charged even when the work was finished before the date.
  • If the owner is found guilty and does not appeal, fix the problem or pay, a Notice of Judgment is filed with the recorder of mortgages 30 days after the hearing. That filing is a lien and lets the city clean up the property or seize it for sheriff's sale.

The city can cut lots, send a property to sheriff's sale or demolish a building. Sale proceeds first cover liens, taxes and sale costs, and any remainder goes to the former owner.

sections.h2: Can a lien be reduced before you sell?
sections.html:
Sometimes. The city runs a Lien Reduction Program for owners who have done significant work to fix violations, with firm limits.

  • Abatement must be finished before the application, and photos must be dated and time stamped.
  • Liens that were adjudicated or sold at tax sale, liens that were foreclosed on, and paid liens cannot be reduced.
  • Demolition and grass liens can only have interest reduced.
  • Reductions are made per violation, there is no entitlement to one, and there are no appeals. The goal is a response within 30 days.
  • If you pay the lien before the application is processed, the application is denied and the payment is not refunded.

That last rule matters on a closing timeline. Ask the department about a lien payoff and about reduction before any payoff is wired. Forms go to 1340 Poydras Street, Suite 1100, or by email with photos attached, under 25 MB per message.

A past as a short term rental can change how a house sells. Short term rentals are not legal in New Orleans without a permit, and the rules sit in both the municipal code and the Comprehensive Zoning Ordinance. New regulations passed on March 23, 2023 took effect July 1, 2023.

Short term rental licenses are not transferable, so a buyer cannot simply take over your permit. The application for a residential short term rental owner permit also asks the owner to certify that the dwelling has no outstanding property taxes or city liens on the lot of record.

If you ran an unpermitted rental, the city can send the case to an administrative adjudication hearing, where a hearing officer may impose fines or revoke permits. Clear that history up with the city before you put a closing date on the calendar.

sections.h2: Property tax bills at a sale
sections.html:
The Orleans Parish Assessor sets the assessment and approves exemptions such as the homestead exemption, then certifies the roll to the city Treasurer, who sends the bills. For questions about a valuation, call the assessor at (504) 754-8811.

Bills have gone out online and by mail in January, with payment due by the end of February. Call the Treasury for the current schedule. Assessment appeals go to the Board of Review, which has met at Delgado Community College's City Park campus in the fall, and the City Council's appeals page lists the dates each year.

Closing agents normally prorate the current year's bill between buyer and seller. If the bill is unpaid, ask for a payoff or tax certificate early.

sections.h2: When a cash sale makes sense
sections.html:
A cash sale fits best when the trouble is the house or the calendar. Common examples here are a vacant inherited house with a code case, a property with a lien the owner cannot finance away, a storm-damaged building a lender will not appraise, or a rental that lost its permit.

A cash buyer purchases the property as it stands, so there is no appraisal contingency, no lender repair demands and no showings. You still need clear title, so the lien, tax and recording points above apply to every route. Compare any cash offer against what a listing would net, and ask what each route leaves you after liens and the documentary tax.

faqs.q: Do I need to fix code violations before selling a house in New Orleans?
faqs.a: Not always, but open violations can lead to a hearing and a lien, and a lien must be paid or released at closing. Fixing the cited items before a hearing can end the case without further city action.

faqs.q: Who pays the documentary transaction tax on a New Orleans sale?
faqs.a: The seller is one of the parties responsible. The tax is a flat $325 for most documents, paid when the act is recorded.

faqs.q: Where do I record a deed or act of sale in New Orleans?
faqs.a: At the Land Records Division of the Orleans Parish Clerk of Civil District Court, 1340 Poydras Street, 4th Floor. It is open Monday to Friday from 8:30 AM to 5:00 PM.

faqs.q: Can I sell a New Orleans house that has an unpermitted short term rental history?
faqs.a: Yes, but the city can pursue unpermitted rentals through adjudication, and permits do not transfer to a buyer. Resolve open cases and any unpaid taxes or liens first.

faqs.q: What if a New Orleans house is in an inherited succession?
faqs.a: Title still has to be sorted out before a sale. The code process researches every person with a legal interest in the property, so an unopened succession can slow a hearing or a sale. Talk to a Louisiana attorney or notary about it.
